items.explainer: A decision model is not a chatbot. You give it an input and a list of closed questions (yes/no, pick one of up to 255 choices, or a rubric score), and it scores every option in one pass and returns a confidence for each instead of writing text. Gemini Decision 1 takes text, images, audio, video and PDFs, answers up to 1,000 questions per request in about 150 to 250 ms, and charges $0.10 per million input tokens with free output. It joins TypeSafe's Jev, which is cheaper and text only.
items.title: Google enters the decision model market with Gemini Decision 1
items.why: Rubric scoring and routing are where schools first use AI, and this makes them cheap enough to run on every submission, which raises the question of who audits the scores.

items.explainer: llama.cpp is the open-source engine that runs language models on your own laptop, and many local-AI apps sit on top of it. Version 1.0 promises a stable API: breaking changes now require a new major version number. It also ships official packages through Homebrew, conda-forge, Docker and an iOS/macOS framework, and supports more than 150 model architectures.
items.title: llama.cpp reaches v1.0.0
items.why: Running a model locally keeps student data on the machine, and a stable engine makes that easier to recommend to schools that cannot send data to a cloud service.

items.explainer: She ran the same instructional-design tasks through Claude Fable 5.2 and the cheaper Sonnet 5.5, and raters scored the output blind against a 24-skill standard. The frontier model won on diagnosis, checking content against its source, and drafting a full storyboard. When a written standard or finished storyboard existed, the cheaper model reached the same verdicts at about a quarter of the cost.
items.title: Is a frontier model worth the cost for course design? A blind test
items.why: Her rule of thumb (pay for judgment, save on checking against a standard you wrote) is a ready answer when a client or colleague asks which model to buy.

policy.blurb: The memo sets rules for the AI tools used with university information, leaves classroom AI rules to faculty, and asks staff to move off personal ChatGPT accounts to the enterprise license by the end of the fall semester.
policy.title: University of Nebraska sets system-wide AI rules (Executive Memorandum 48)

tryThisWeek.steps: Take one handout and its source reading, change three facts in the handout, and ask two models (one frontier, one cheaper) to check the handout against the source. Count planted errors caught and new errors invented, and you have a 30-minute test of whether that task needs the expensive model.
tryThisWeek.title: Plant three errors, then pick your model

items.explainer: An XY problem is when someone wants X, assumes method Y will get them there, and asks only about Y. XYBench is a set of 8,115 such questions that checks whether an assistant notices the mistaken assumption and steers toward the real goal. On its Stack Overflow questions, five models made the real goal the focus of their answer 35 to 41% of the time, yet picked the goal-focused answer 71 to 84% of the time when shown two to choose from.
items.title: XYBench: models can spot the helpful answer but rarely write it
items.why: Students ask XY questions all day, and a tutor bot that answers the literal question is the default behavior unless you prompt against it.

items.explainer: Speakers and attendees of the AI Engineer Code Summit wrote a manifesto modeled on the 2001 Agile Manifesto. It defines slop as putting less effort into producing something than you ask the reader to spend understanding it, and says using AI does not by itself make work slop. Its resolutions include labeling agent-written text, checking the parts that matter before sending, and telling a colleague kindly when they send you slop.
items.title: The No AI Slop Manifesto
items.why: The definition is about effort, not about AI, so it works as a classroom norm and as a one-page starting point for a team policy.

items.explainer: OpenAI describes Wallet as a way for its agents to complete purchases with user approval and existing card protections. Latent Space reports the agent never sees the card number and that it works through Amex, Mastercard and Visa. In plain words: the assistant can now finish the checkout, and the person approves the charge.
items.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy things with your approval
items.why: Once an agent can spend, the question for a school or client shifts from what it can write to what it is allowed to approve.

tryThisWeek.steps: Paste three real questions students asked you last week into your AI assistant, exactly as asked, and note whether it answers the literal question or the real goal. Then add one line ("Before you answer, say what I am probably trying to achieve, and if my approach is not the best way, lead with the better way") and run them again. It takes about 20 minutes and shows you what a student gets by default.
tryThisWeek.title: Ask the question behind the question

items.explainer: Stanford's AI Hub for Education reviewed the 52 randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies in its repository of 1,686 papers on AI in education. A randomized trial assigns students to use a tool or not by chance, so differences in learning can be traced to the tool. Across the 52, students who used AI for support, such as explanations or practice problems, generally learned more than students who used it to complete their work, though neither use was consistently positive.
items.source: Education Week / Stanford AI Hub for Education
items.title: 52 real tests out of 1,686 papers: what the evidence on AI and learning says
items.why: It gives a teacher one evidence-backed rule for designing AI use: point the tool at practice and explanation, not at producing the graded work.

items.explainer: IBM released preview Granite 4.1 models (3B and 8B) trained on LLMON, a markup format whose six structural delimiters are reserved special tokens that never appear in ordinary text. Every block of instructions, data or requirements gets an ID, and an exec block says which instructions apply to which data, much like passing arguments to a function. IBM reports it resists prompt injection, where text inside a document hijacks the model, far better than plain prompts, though these are IBM's own benchmarks on experimental models.
items.title: LLMON: a markup language built into the model to separate instructions from data
items.why: Any AI tool that reads student work, email or web pages can be steered by hidden text in that content, and this is the first serious attempt to fix it inside the model rather than in the prompt.

items.explainer: Potkalitsky argues that the open question about AI has shifted from what the systems are to whether they can speed up their own development, a process called recursive self-improvement. He points to an Anthropic report saying Claude wrote more than 80% of the code merged into its production codebase by May 2026, while Pew polling shows public concern stuck at 52% since 2023. His point is that insiders may notice a change well before the public or schools do.
items.title: AI is getting weird again
items.why: It is a clear, sourced way to explain to faculty why AI guidance written a year ago may already be out of date.

tryThisWeek.steps: Pick one assignment where students now use AI to produce part of the work. Rewrite the AI step so the tool only explains a concept or generates five practice items, and students write the graded piece themselves. Ask them afterward which version helped them remember more.
tryThisWeek.title: Move one AI task from doing to practicing

items.explainer: Physicists simulate particle physics by placing fields on a grid of points in spacetime, called a lattice, but the Standard Model's left-handed and right-handed particles have long resisted a clean lattice definition. Physicist Nathaniel Craig says he set the strategy and the model turned it into a concrete construction and a detailed proof, including a way to carry field configurations onto ever finer grids. Craig calls the result a candidate that is more an answer in principle than in practice.
items.title: GPT-6 Astra helped build a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model
items.why: It is the clearest current example of a model doing the proof steps while a human expert sets direction and outside specialists check the work, a pattern worth showing any faculty group.

items.explainer: Tom Solid shows a setup where several Claude Code Desktop sessions, each with its own context, send messages to one another. It is a small multi-agent system: one session can hand a task to another and get a result back instead of one long conversation doing everything.
items.title: Claude Code Desktop sessions that message each other
items.why: Multi-session setups are what most organizations will ask about next, and this is a plain-language demo to point them to.

items.explainer: LVMH's media arm, which owns several European newspapers and magazines, will use AI in its newsrooms and make its publications more accessible through ChatGPT. Deals like this decide which journalism a chatbot can draw on and cite when it answers a question.
items.title: LVMH's media division partners with OpenAI
items.why: Students increasingly meet the news through a chatbot answer, so knowing which publishers sit behind those answers is a source-literacy lesson.

policy.blurb: Executive Memorandum 48, dated Nov. 1, covers chatbots, coding, transcription and research tools, requires human review and disclosure of material AI contributions, and leaves course expectations with faculty; staff on personal ChatGPT accounts are asked to move to the university's enterprise account by the end of fall.
policy.title: University of Nebraska sets one acceptable-use policy for all AI systems

tryThisWeek.steps: Pick a tiny classroom need, such as a page that shows where your students' favorite musicians come from on a map. Write one detailed prompt to a coding assistant describing the data, the page and what a click should do, then note what worked first time and what needed a second prompt. Simon Willison built a full map plugin mostly this way this weekend.
tryThisWeek.title: Build one small tool from one prompt

items.explainer: Fable 5.2 is Anthropic's new top model tier, priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, generating up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1. Benchmarks are mixed: large gains on long, hard tasks like the Remote Labor Index, while Opus 5.5 still wins where a judge grades a finished deliverable. Anthropic itself advises defaulting to Opus 5.5 and moving up only for the hardest technical work.
items.source: Don't Worry About the Vase (Zvi Mowshowitz)
items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 is out: cheaper, faster, and aimed at the hardest jobs
items.why: For consulting, the useful message is model routing: most school and office work does not need the biggest model, and paying for it by default wastes budget.

items.explainer: FrontierML gives an AI agent a 12 hour sandbox, a $10, $50 or $200 wallet and 21 machine learning tasks, then scores the model it ships on a hidden test set. A human researcher gained 56 points with $10 and 66.1 with $200; the best agent, Opus 5.5, gained 45.4 and 58.8. The same issue covers RSI Control Arena, where models given a hidden side task while training a successor completed it in 48 percent of 374 attack runs.
items.title: FrontierML: agents that turn a cash budget into better models
items.why: It is a concrete way to show students and clients that agents now plan, spend and build, and that monitoring them is still imperfect.

items.explainer: OpenAI says it is widening its academic program to give 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to its frontier models. Alongside it, OpenAI published a study of how more than 1,800 scientists use ChatGPT in daily research work. Both are vendor announcements, so the usage claims come from the company itself.
items.title: ChatGPT for Academic Researchers expands to 200,000 researchers
items.why: Free frontier access for faculty changes the procurement conversation on campuses that are writing enterprise AI rules right now.

policy.blurb: The memo separates platform approval from permission to use a tool in a course, keeps assignment decisions with faculty, requires disclosure of substantive AI help, and asks staff on personal ChatGPT accounts to move to the enterprise account by the end of fall 2026.
policy.title: University of Nebraska sets campus rules for AI tools (Executive Memorandum 48)

tryThisWeek.steps: Pick one task you repeat every week, such as drafting feedback comments or summarizing a reading. Run it on a small fast model and on a top model, hide which is which, and pick the better output. If the small model wins or ties, you have just found a cheaper default.
tryThisWeek.title: Run a two-model routing test on one real task

items.explainer: Detectors are models too, and they fail when new chatbots or humanizer tools change what AI text looks like. Researchers at Cornell Tech and MIT used test-time adaptation: the detector keeps adjusting its own parameters on new, unlabeled text it is shown, instead of staying frozen after training.
items.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
items.why: Any teacher tempted to trust a detector score should know how badly frozen detectors miss disguised text.

items.explainer: OpenAI released a frontier model (Astra) and an efficient everyday model (Sol). Astra drops to $8 input and $40 output per million tokens, and cached input falls to $0.40, which makes long agent sessions that reread the same context much cheaper.
items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol
items.why: Cheaper cached context changes the cost math for anyone building course tools on top of these models.

items.explainer: Instead of letting an AI agent run code on your laptop, you send that code to a separate disposable machine. If the code misbehaves, the damage stays in the sandbox.
items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.why: A simple safety habit worth teaching to anyone experimenting with agents in class or in consulting.

policy.blurb: The CU system policy requires disclosure when generative AI contributes to university decisions, a model other campuses may borrow.
policy.title: University of Colorado explains its AI disclosure rule

tryThisWeek.steps: Write one short paragraph yourself, ask a chatbot for one on the same prompt, then ask it to rewrite that one to sound human. Paste all three into any AI detector you have access to and note which ones it flags. Bring the results to a colleague conversation about detector policy.
tryThisWeek.title: Run your own detector stress test

items.explainer: Neon is Google's new middle model in the Gemini 4 family, between the heavy Carbon model and the fast Hydrogen model. It has a 1 million token context window and costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15. Google reports a 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its highest thinking setting.
items.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon
items.why: A mid-priced model that scores near the top changes which model you would recommend to a school on a budget.

items.explainer: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 release comes in two versions, Astra and Sol, and early reports say they score higher while costing far less per benchmark run. Early testers disagree about what Astra is like to work with day to day.
items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol lower benchmark costs
items.why: When two labs cut prices in the same week, cost stops being the main reason a campus avoids AI tools.

items.explainer: Genie is a world model: you describe or show a scene and it generates an explorable, interactive environment frame by frame. Version 4 is now open for people to try rather than a research preview.
items.title: Genie 4 is now available
items.why: Generated, walkable worlds are a new kind of creative prompt for visual and music classes.

policy.blurb: Regents postponed a vote on the system-wide AI Engaged statement to February after faculty objected that Claude wrote the first draft and that this came out late. Campuses will draft their own policies meanwhile.
policy.title: University of Alaska delays its AI statement after faculty learn an AI drafted it

tryThisWeek.steps: Take one real class task, such as feedback on a 300 word paragraph, and estimate the tokens in and out. Multiply by the published per million token prices for two or three models, including Gemini 4 Neon. Note how cheap a full semester of that task is, and whether the cheaper model's output is good enough.
tryThisWeek.title: Price one assignment across three models
